title: Proactive heartbeat latching to preserve tool-call ordering across SSE reconnects
creator: Asha Patel
description: Introduce a lightweight heartbeat-latch mechanism for server-sent event (SSE) responses that anchors function/tool-call boundaries and enables deterministic reassembly on client reconnects. The goal is to reduce ordering and duplication violations for function-calls when clients lose connection and later resume, without requiring heavyweight session state or changing existing SDK APIs.
design_notes: Problem: existing reconnect strategies rely on resume tokens or idempotent chunk ids, which either increase payload overhead or require client state that many legacy ReadableStream-based clients do not maintain.

Proposal: emit short-lived 'latch' heartbeat events at semantic boundaries (pre-toolcall, post-toolcall finalization). Each latch carries a compact latch-id and sequence anchor. On reconnect, client provides last-received-latch and server replays frames deterministically from the next anchor.

Key primitives: (1) latch-id (8-12 char opaque token), (2) anchor-seq (monotonic chunk index per stream), (3) optional hint header X-Stream-Latch: <latch-id>:<anchor-seq> sent by client on reconnect to bias replay.

Compatibility: fallbacks for clients that cannot send header: server uses last-known sequence derived from ephemeral checkpoint store tied to connection id and a TTL. No hard API-breaking changes required for SDKs; SDKs can opt-in to attach the header for faster resync.

Backpressure considerations: latch heartbeat cadence tuned to logical boundaries rather than time; small streams may not emit latches often, so we also allow a periodic (configurable) keepalive when no boundary has been crossed for >2s to bound replay window.

Tradeoffs: reduces replay ambiguity at the cost of extra lightweight heartbeat events and an ephemeral checkpoint store on the server. Avoid locking long-term per-client state by using TTL and best-effort eviction.
Security/privacy: latch tokens are opaque and rotate per-stream. Do not include PII. Checkpoints are TTL-limited and scrubbed on model/version rollouts.
Observability: emit metrics for latch-gap-frequency, replay-success-rate, duplicate-toolcall-rate after reconnect, and latch-emission-latency.

Interoperability: supports both plain SSE over HTTP/1.1 and EventStream over HTTP/2; we will implement a shim for older clients that expect JSONL boundaries by emitting a short JSON payload for latch events with type: "latch".
acceptance_criteria: Reconnect with X-Stream-Latch header causes server to replay starting after provided anchor in 95% of tests across synthetic loss scenarios.
Tool/function-calls emitted pre-latch or post-latch are delivered in the same order after reconnect in 99% of deterministic unit tests.
No API-breaking changes required for existing SDKs; opt-in header works with updated SDKs but older SDKs still receive correct output with slightly larger replay window.
Production telemetry shows decreased duplicate-toolcall incidents by >= 50% for affected customers in controlled rollout.
Benchmarked additional bandwidth overhead from latch events is <0.3% for representative workloads.
implementation_plan: Server: implement latch generator in event-stream runtime that inserts latch events at configured semantic boundaries and as periodic keepalives.
Server: add ephemeral checkpoint store keyed by connection id + model-version with small TTL (default 60s) to map last emitted anchor -> offset.
API: accept optional X-Stream-Latch reconnect hint header; if present, attempt fast-path replay from anchor; otherwise fallback to checkpoint TTL lookup.
SDK: add optional flag in Node/Python SDKs to attach last-latch header on reconnect; provide utility in SDKs for reading latch events and storing last-latch locally.
Client: implement readme guidance for legacy clients (ReadableStream) describing best-effort header attachment and how to handle latch events in stream parsing.
Testing: create fault-injection harness simulating mid-stream disconnects at tool-call boundaries, and assert replay ordering/deduplication.
Rollout: start with non-critical internal customers and canary region, collect metrics before wider rollout.
rollout_plan: Canary: enable latch emission on 3 internal teams' namespaces for 48h (observability + manual verification).
Stage: enable in us-west-2 for 5% of hosted traffic and enable SDK opt-ins; monitor duplicate-toolcall-rate and latency regressions for 72h.
Gradual: expand to 25% -> 60% -> 100% with 24h observation gates and automated rollback on regressions.
Dedicated/Private: feature flag exposed to Dedicated control plane; Private customers can opt-in after upgrade and offer a migration guide.
review_notes: Security review requested: ensure latch token generation and checkpoint TTL satisfy data-retention policy.
Design review with Runtime and SDK teams 2025-08-22: agreed opt-in header approach to minimize impact on legacy clients.
Perf review 2025-08-28: initial microbench shows <1% CPU overhead in hot path; memory overhead dominated by checkpoint TTL table which will be sized and sharded.
updates: 2025-08-15: Ticket created. Initial design sketch and tradeoffs documented.
2025-08-22: Design review completed with Runtime and SDK. Decided on 8-12 char opaque latch tokens and TTL-based checkpoint fallback.
2025-08-30: Server-side latch emitter prototype landed on feature branch. Basic tests for latch emission and JSONL shim added.
2025-09-01: SDK helpers for Node and Python completed. Added opt-in flag and example reconnect handler.
2025-09-03: Canary rollout plan drafted. Preparing observability dashboards and fault injection harness for canary.
notes_for_followup: Investigate persistent checkpoint option for long-running streams ( > 10m ) and its cost tradeoffs.
Consider exposing diagnostics endpoint for customers to debug latch-anchor mismatches during private deployment upgrades.
Post-rollout: gather client SDK adoption metrics and consider making header attachment the default in next major SDK release.
